findings.quote: A smaller $c$ gives a larger $\Delta T$ only when the heat and the mass are the same.
findings.problem: Read literally, the "only when" is false. With equal heat, a smaller-c sample that also has less mass still has the larger temperature change (for example 1 kg of water, c = 4186, against 0.5 kg of oil, c = 2000, each given 4186 J: 1 °C against about 4.2 °C). The intended meaning, that c alone decides the comparison only when Q and m are equal, is right. The trap's own warning line, Q/(mc), covers the counterexample, so the harm is small. The base said "for the same heat input and the same mass" with no "only".
findings.source: Reader rules, Sol-audit boundary test; severity follows the lead's final-run ruling on lesson-chemistry-thermodynamics-and-kinetics (a counterexample covered by the lesson's own rule is Minor)

findings.problem: Core Concept defines $\Delta T=T_f-T_i$ and says cooling gives $Q<0$. The calorimetry example then writes the hot water's heat as $(80-T_f)$, a positive amount lost, without saying so. The equation and the answer are correct, and step 4 shows the hot water losing heat over a 40 °C drop. But no clause links the signed Q of Core Concept to the positive "heat lost" used here. A student who keeps $T_f-T_i$ on both sides gets $T_f=-40$ °C.
findings.source: content-checklist L19 (solution steps shown); LSG Examples section

findings.quote: If heat leaves the system, $Q<0$. If the surroundings do work on the system, such as squeezing a gas, $W<0$. Some books define $W$ as work done on the system and write $\Delta U=Q+W$. Always check which convention a question uses.
findings.problem: This paragraph has five sentences, over the one-to-three limit. The Conduction paragraph (four sentences) and the Specific Heat Capacity definition paragraph (four sentences) also run over.
